practicalQuestion: When symptoms and clinic-based measures have normalized but high-speed and sport-specific exposure remain incomplete, how should physical therapy and performance staff structure the next 7–10 days and define progress, hold, or regress criteria without relying on a single return-to-sport cutoff?

decisionContext.population: Collegiate athlete nearing unrestricted participation after a lower-extremity injury
decisionContext.sport: Field sport with sprinting, cutting, and reactive demands
decisionContext.phase: Modified participation to unrestricted team activity
decisionContext.outcome: Coordinate staged exposure and decision ownership across rehabilitation and performance staff
decisionContext.constraints: Limited practice opportunities; competition schedule continues; no athlete-identifying or diagnosis-specific data

evidenceConfidence.rationale: No source tests a 7 to 10 day structure or progress, hold or regress criteria for athletes nearing unrestricted participation. The pack offers indirect pieces: an ACL reconstruction case series comparing on-field rehabilitation loads with team and match demands, a single-player case study, retrospective and observational data on near-maximal speed exposure in healthy professional players, a practitioner survey, and digest summaries. Sources partly disagree on whether between-limb asymmetry should guide progression, and on how near-maximal speed exposure relates to injury and strength.

dimensions.sourceReview: Every claim is checked against original source text. Designs are a 100-player case series, a single-player case study, a retrospective multi-team analysis, an observational cohort of 58 players, a practitioner survey, and research digest summaries of a meta-analysis and of an article on asymmetries.
dimensions.directness: Indirect. Only the ACL case series and case study describe the late-stage transition, and neither tests decision criteria. Speed exposure data come from healthy players and match hamstring injuries, not athletes returning from injury.
dimensions.consistency: Mixed. Field work matching team training but not match demands is consistent. Asymmetry use and the effects of near-maximal speed exposure show tension.
dimensions.transferability: Low to moderate. Populations are mostly male professional or amateur soccer players, with some Gaelic football data cited secondhand. No collegiate, female, or non-ACL, non-hamstring returning athletes are studied.

bottomLine.text: The evidence does not test a 7 to 10 day plan or a single set of progress, hold or regress rules. It does suggest that controlled field work can approach team training loads but stays below match play, especially for decelerations, that total distance alone is not a useful progression metric, and that practitioners already use several criteria rather than one. Near-maximal speed exposure timing and frequency show associations with hamstring outcomes in healthy players, but these are not causal and were not studied in returning athletes.

actions.title: Option: benchmark each exposure metric against team and match references
actions.text: In an ACL reconstruction case series in male soccer players, final-stage field work reached about team training levels for total distance, high-intensity distance and accelerations, but only 48% of team training deceleration distance and 26% to 82% of match values across metrics. Total distance plateaued and the authors judged it not a useful metric. Staff could track high-intensity distance, peak speed, accelerations and decelerations separately against the athlete's own team training and match references.

actions.title: Option: schedule near-maximal speed exposures deliberately
actions.text: In retrospective data from healthy elite soccer players, no match hamstring injuries occurred when exposures above 95% of maximal sprinting speed happened two days before a match, but the authors urge caution. In another cohort, more weekly efforts above 90% of maximum velocity were weakly linked with declines in eccentric hamstring strength. Staff could plan when near-maximal exposures occur relative to the next session or match, rather than letting them happen only in practice. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): with limited practice days, decide in advance which day carries the near-maximal exposure.

actions.title: Option: define progress, hold and regress using a multi-criterion panel
actions.text: Surveyed physical therapists used several criteria for release to team training, including strength, sprint and high-speed running, intense actions, pain and GPS workload. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): progress when the planned exposure is completed with stable criteria, hold when one criterion shifts, and regress when symptoms or several criteria worsen. Agree these definitions across rehabilitation and performance staff before the block starts.

actions.title: Option: use team training as the intermediate step and avoid exposure spikes
actions.text: Match play carries higher hamstring injury incidence than training in field sports, players with less match time accumulate less weekly load, and infrequent or over-exposure is described as a workload spike linked with injury. Staff could close the gap to match demands through modified then full team training before competition, adding exposure gradually. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): name one owner for each daily progression decision and record who signs off each step.

monitoring.label: External load by metric
monitoring.text: Track high-intensity distance, peak speed, acceleration and deceleration distance against team training and match references, rather than total distance alone.

monitoring.label: Near-maximal speed exposures
monitoring.text: Count efforts above 90% and above 95% of the athlete's maximum velocity and record the day they occur relative to the next match.

monitoring.label: Eccentric hamstring strength trend
monitoring.text: In professional male soccer players, higher weekly sprint distance and efforts above 90% of maximum velocity were weakly associated with drops in eccentric hamstring strength, so a trend measure could sit alongside speed exposure counts.

monitoring.label: Between-limb asymmetry, interpreted cautiously
monitoring.text: A case study used step impulse asymmetry to guide phase progression, but a digest summary reports no evidence that asymmetries increase injury risk. Treat asymmetry as one input, not a gate.

guardrails.text: This brief informs criteria and monitoring only. Progression, competition and clearance decisions stay with the treating clinicians and the athlete's medical team.
The speed-timing findings are associations from retrospective data in healthy elite players. Do not treat a specific day or exposure count as a protective rule for a returning athlete.
The diagnosis is not known here. ACL and hamstring findings should not be applied as injury-specific rules to a different lower-extremity injury.

Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): because matches carry higher hamstring injury incidence than training, first competitive exposure deserves a planned role and minutes discussion rather than defaulting to full participation.

limitations.text: Studied populations are mostly male professional or amateur soccer players, with Gaelic football data cited secondhand. None are collegiate or female.

Designs are a case series without a control group, a single case study, retrospective and observational analyses, a practitioner survey, and digest summaries. None compare one progression approach with another.
The survey describes which criteria practitioners use, not which criteria predict safe return or reinjury.

whatCouldChange.text: Prospective studies in collegiate field-sport athletes that compare criteria panels for the final transition against outcomes such as reinjury or time to full participation.
Replication of the near-maximal speed timing findings in athletes returning from injury, ideally beyond retrospective association.

evidenceTension.text: A single-player ACL case study describes step impulse asymmetries as usable to guide phase progression, while a digest summary concludes there is no evidence that asymmetries increase injury risk. Separately, near-maximal speed exposure is associated with fewer match hamstring injuries in some data, yet more weekly efforts above 90% of maximum velocity were weakly linked with lower eccentric hamstring strength in another cohort. These tensions are not resolved for returning collegiate athletes.

claims.text: In this case series of 100 male amateur and professional soccer players after ACL reconstruction, 97 had follow-up and 84% returned to competition (100% of professionals, 80% of amateurs). The authors conclude that completing all five on-field stages almost prepared players for team training demands, but workloads remained low compared with match play.

assumptions: The specific injury is unknown, so ACL and hamstring evidence is treated as indirect for a general lower-extremity injury.
The field sport's sprinting, cutting and reactive demands are assumed broadly comparable to soccer for load-metric purposes.
Speed-percentage monitoring assumes the athlete has a known or measurable individual maximum velocity.
coverageGaps: No study testing how to structure the final 7 to 10 days between modified and unrestricted participation
No validated progress, hold or regress criteria linked to outcomes such as reinjury or performance
No collegiate or female athlete data for the late return-to-sport transition
No evidence on how to divide decision ownership between rehabilitation and performance staff
No dosing evidence for cutting and reactive exposure during the final transition
No evidence for lower-extremity injuries other than ACL reconstruction and hamstring strain
